data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological survival is descriptive/causal; scientific preference is normative/methodological.","Organisms do not choose to be tested; scientists actively seek severe tests.","Evolution has no goal of 'truth'; science has the regulative ideal of verisimilitude."],"overturn_conditions":["If biological survival were shown to be purely random with no correlation to fitness, the analogy would fail.","If scientific progress were shown to rely on inductive accumulation rather than conjecture and refutation."],"shared_structure":["Elimination of unfit variants leads to survival of the remaining.","Survival is retrospective, not predictive of future environment changes.","Preference is based on past performance under stress, not inherent probability of correctness."],"source_memory_refs":["evolutionary_selection_process","critical_rationality_framework"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we prefer the organism that survived a plague for breeding without assuming it is immune to all future diseases, we prefer the corroborated theory without assuming it is probable.","The 'fitness' of a theory is its capacity to withstand falsification, analogous to an organism's resistance to environmental stressors."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a methodological rule for selecting the most 'testable' and 'informative' target for falsification, thereby maximizing verisimilitude (truth-likeness) without assigning probability. This stance survives the charge of smuggling induction only if one accepts the cost of abandoning any guarantee of practical reliability for action, reducing scientific preference to a bet on where error is most likely to be found rather than where truth is most likely to reside.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd-Miller proof demonstrates that verisimilitude cannot be coherently defined for false theories, then the goal of maximizing verisimilitude becomes unintelligible, collapsing the defense.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on' a theory (e.g., engineering) inherently requires an assumption of reliability that corroboration cannot provide without induction, then the preference is pragmatically indefensible on Popperian terms.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the analogy to natural selection is interpreted as providing a normative justification rather than a descriptive explanation of survival, it commits the naturalistic fallacy Popper sought to avoid.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument reconstructs Popper's distinction between 'probability' (logical likelihood based on content) and 'corroboration' (historical record of surviving severe tests). It posits that preferring a highly corroborated theory is rational because high corroboration indicates high empirical content and thus high testability. By choosing the theory with the highest content that has not yet been falsified, scientists maximize the potential growth of knowledge (verisimilitude) even if the theory is false. The mechanism relies on the normative rule: 'Always test the boldiest conjecture,' which justifies preference without implying the conjecture is probable to be true or to remain unfalsified.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
